column8: Two properties must be distinguished.  The coverage of unfolded intervals is the rate at which they contain the true cross section.  The calibration of a test is the rate at which it rejects a true hypothesis.  Calibration can be obtained without validated intervals by simulating the whole analysis chain at the hypothesis, so that the estimator's bias enters the simulated null distribution.  A calibration obtained in this way is valid to the extent that the simulated chain reproduces the analysis of the data.  Unfolded results can be compared with any prediction at truth level without simulating each generator through the detector. For hypothesis tests the advantage is smaller.  A test at reconstruction level would avoid the regularization bias, but it would still need the same response model.  Each external prediction would have to be folded through the analysis simulation's response, which is the hybrid construction of \S\ref{sec:joint5d-design}, with the same composition below the fine grid.  The tests of this section instead calibrate the unfolded statistic in simulation, so that the bias enters the null distribution rather than the decision.  We have not compared their power with that of a reconstruction-level test.

column8: For each of five predictions $G$ (the MINERvA Tune~v1, GENIE~2.12.10 without and with MEC, NuWro~21.09 and GiBUU~2019; \S\ref{sec:eavailw-band}), the null $H_{0}(G)$ is that the true cross section equals $G$ on every cell of a fine five-dimensional grid. Below that grid, the null truth has the MINERvA Tune~v1 simulation's event composition, varied in each pseudo-experiment by the drawn interaction-model universes. Every fine-cell integral is held fixed in that variation. The background is the Tune~v1 simulation's, with its uncertainty bands. This \emph{hybrid null} is the hypothesis the calibration simulates. For the Tune~v1, which is the analysis simulation itself, no external prediction is combined with the Tune~v1 composition. Three requirements are distinct. The hybrid null is defined exactly on the finite grid, and no convergence is needed to define it. Whether it represents the physical generator prediction depends on condition~(i) (\S\ref{sec:joint5d-conditions}). Whether the calibration reproduces the analysis of the data is calibration fidelity (conditions~(ii)--(iv)). Each prediction is tested in total (rate and shape together) and in shape alone: \jtNtests{} tests. The fine grid is the analysis binning of \S\ref{sec:method-binning}, $14\times16\times7\times7\times6$ bins in $(\pT,\pPar,\Eavail,q_{3},W)$; the test cells below are its integrals.

column8: The tests are evaluated on a coarse $3^{5}$ grid in $(\pT,\pPar,\Eavail,q_{3},W)$ with edges $\pT\in[0,0.55,0.85,4.5]\,\si{GeV/c}$, $\pPar\in[1.5,3.5,6,60]\,\si{GeV/c}$, $\Eavail\in[0,0.4,1.5,100]\,\si{GeV}$, $q_{3}\in[0,1.2,2,100]\,\si{GeV}$ and $W\in[0,1.4,2.2,100]\,\si{GeV}$. That distribution is taken from the development simulation. The tests are restricted to the \jtNcells{} supported cells (J). For GiBUU, whose sample lacks high-energy neutrinos, the domain is the \jtNcellsGiBUU{} cells with $\pPar<\SI{6}{GeV/c}$. The grid specifies a finite hybrid hypothesis and a reporting statistic. column8: Two statistics are formed from the unfolded cell values $F$ and the prediction $\mu_{G}$. The total (rate-and-shape) statistic is $T_{\mathrm{tot}}=r^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}r$ with $r=F-\mu_{G}$. The shape statistic $T_{\mathrm{sh}}$ has the same form on the normalized cell fractions, with the normalization Jacobian applied to $\Sigma$ and one cell dropped. The metric $\Sigma=V+\mathrm{diag}\,\mathrm{Var}(\mu_{G})$ adds the prediction's own finite-sample variance to $V$. Here $V$ is a Ledoit--Wolf-shrunk covariance~\cite{LedoitWolf:2004} of \jtVn{} pilot pseudo-experiments at the Tune~v1 null. The metric defines how hypotheses are compared, and so it affects power. The null calibration below, not the metric, sets each test's size.

column8: The prediction variance is diagonal because each simulated event of a prediction falls in one cell. column8: The data are unfolded once, with the full simulation. The Monte Carlo $p$ value of a test is $(k+1)/(B+1)$, where $k$ of $B$ null pseudo-experiments reach the observed statistic. This $p$ value is never zero. The $p$ value on which each decision rests, the \emph{claim} $p$ value, is the largest over the specified \emph{claim variants}, which shift the null. The variants move it by an upper bound on the simulation-size difference between the pseudo-experiments and the data unfold (condition~(iv), \S\ref{sec:joint5d-conditions}), and by $\pm\jtMoneKappa\,\delta_{\mathrm{fine}}$ (condition~(i)). The external nulls are strongly non-central, with non-centralities $\lambda$ of \jtLambdaMin{}--\jtLambdaMax{} in these units. They are non-central because the calibration reproduces the estimator's pull toward its prior (\S\ref{sec:val-departure}). column8: The ten tests are carried out with the Holm procedure~\cite{Holm:1979} at familywise level $\alpha=\jtAlpha$. A determinacy requirement also applies: a step rejects only when the 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval~\cite{Clopper:1934} of $k/B$ lies entirely below its Holm threshold. Calibration proceeded in batches of \jtBatch{} pseudo-experiments per null, to at most \jtBcap{}, under a sequential rule that stopped a null once both of its decisions were determined. A null stopped when a 99.5\% Clopper--Pearson interval of $k/B$ lay entirely on one side of each of its thresholds and met a fixed precision requirement. The decision rule uses the upper end of the two-sided 95\% interval, a one-sided 97.5\% upper bound.

column8: Two assumptions are made: (A1) each true null's calibrated tail probability is uniformly distributed or conservative, and (A2) the pseudo-experiments' exceedances are independent given the data. Under A1 and A2, the probability that this upper end falls below the threshold, at any number of pseudo-experiments up to \jtBcap{}, is below the threshold. This holds whatever rule determines when sampling stops, including the budget extensions. The decision rule therefore controls the familywise error rate of the ten decisions at 5\% under these assumptions. That rate is the probability of falsely rejecting at least one true hypothesis among them. The error control applies only to the decisions. The point estimates $(k+1)/(B+1)$ carry no separate error-control guarantee. Under these assumptions, the bound $\mathrm{FWER}\le0.8902\,\alpha<0.9\,\alpha$ is derived in \S\ref{sec:joint5d-fwer}.

column8: MINERvA's recoil-energy analyses assign a hadronic-energy response uncertainty derived from test-beam calorimetry~\cite{MINERvA:2015testbeam}, separate from the GEANT hadron-interaction reweights~\cite{MINERvA:2021owq,MINERvA:2022incl}. In the low-recoil measurement the resulting hadronic-energy uncertainty rises to \SI{10}{\percent} at its highest three-momentum transfers, $0.9<q_{3}<\SI{1.2}{GeV}$~\cite{MINERvA:2022incl}. The specified nuisance model here includes the reweights but no calorimetric response band. Such a band would act on all five nulls together, through the shared detector simulation and unfolding. A response mismodeling could move each observed statistic in either direction, and a band drawn in the calibration would also broaden and could shift each null distribution. The net effect on each $p$ value is unmeasured. The GENIE~2.12.10 projection result of \S\ref{sec:joint5d-projections} shows that the information rejecting that prediction involves the hadronic axes, on which a response band would act.

column8: In an exploratory sensitivity study of the response~\cite{JointTestRecoil2026}, the data are re-unfolded with the simulation's reconstructed recoil energy scaled by $\pm\SI{4}{\percent}$, and the ten tests are re-evaluated against the null distributions used for the decisions. This scale is the level of data--simulation agreement reported for test-beam protons, pions and electrons of 0.35--\SI{2.0}{GeV/c}~\cite{MINERvA:2015testbeam}. Neutrons and higher-momentum hadrons, which matter at high $W$, lie outside that sample. The $\pm4\%$ scale is not a validated uncertainty prescription. At both $-4\%$ and $+4\%$ every one of the ten rejections holds. Nine tests keep $k=0$. NuWro's shape test, the closest to its null, changes from $k=1$ to $k=3$ of 1751 at $+4\%$ ($p=0.0023$, against a Holm threshold of 0.05). The null distributions were not regenerated with the variation, although they are simulated through the same detector model, so the size of this omission is unmeasured for these strongly non-central nulls. The study also leaves untested particle-species, energy-dependent or resolution effects, a response difference applied before calibration, and larger variations. The rejections are therefore conditional on the simulation's hadronic response, and the response model is not shown to be complete. The observed statistics at each scale, and the study's controls, are given in the records document.
